citation: Kaslow et al. (2021), Mission Engineering and the CubeSat System Reference Model
title: Mission Engineering and the CubeSat System Reference Model
modeling_scope: System-level CubeSat mission/reference model. The CSRM is a SysML-compliant logical space-ground architecture and repository for stakeholders, technical measures, behaviors, requirements, architecture, and validation/verification artifacts; it is intended as a starting point for mission-specific logical and physical CubeSat architectures. Power/energy appears as a trade-study factor, but the paper does not present a dedicated EPS model.
mbse_language_method_tool: Model-Based Systems Engineering using the CubeSat System Reference Model; SysML-compliant; hosted/imported in an unspecified graphical modeling tool; uses stereotypes and model elements for requirements, behaviors, architecture, technical measures, and V&V. Specific tool name not reported.
robot_platform: CubeSat/nanosatellite mission/platform; space and ground segments. No specific CubeSat form factor or named mission is reported.
task_domain: CubeSat mission engineering and mission-specific space-ground system design, including logical architecture, physical architecture, requirements engineering, mission threads, trade studies, interoperability, SoS considerations, and V&V.
interface: Model/tool interface: mission teams download the CSRM specification/files from OMG and import them into their own graphical modeling tool. Model integration interfaces include trace links among stakeholders, requirements, behaviors, architecture, technical measures, and V&V, plus deployer interface requirements shown in the CSRM element overview.
feedback: Trade-study/technical-measure feedback is described: performance levels derived from requirements and technical measures are used to make mission-level decisions and measure decisions against stakeholder needs/objectives. V&V elements also include plan, procedure, conduct, result, and status fields. The paper also solicits stakeholder feedback for extending CSRM.
network_latency_assumptions: Not applicable; downlink data rate and data timeliness are discussed qualitatively, but no latency assumptions are reported.
evaluation: The paper presents a preliminary qualitative assessment mapping CSRM support to Mission Engineering activities and identifies areas needing further research. It also states that the CSRM had been vetted by systems engineering professionals and introduced to the CubeSat mission development community with favorable results, but reports no quantitative evaluation.
rq_relevance: RQ1: yes, because the paper describes a general MBSE/SysML CubeSat logical space-ground reference model and proposed mission-engineering extension; EPS is not modeled in detail, but power/energy is included as a trade-study factor. RQ2: partial, because outcomes such as completeness, reusability, sharing/reuse, and potential mission success are attributed to the CSRM/MBSE approach, but no EPS-specific or quantitative reliability/reproducibility/integrability outcomes are reported. RQ3: partial, because CSRM includes general requirements-to-V&V traceability and Verification/Validation Activity elements with plan/procedure/conduct/result/status fields, but no EPS-specific verification procedure is described.
claimed_outcomes: The MBSE/SysML CSRM is intended to foster completeness and economies of scale associated with reusability.
Use of the CSRM is claimed to establish a mechanism to share and reuse components with other design activities.
The proposed Mission Engineering extension is claimed to have potential value for increasing mission success across the CubeSat developer community.
The CSRM is positioned as a unifying environment for universities to build on each other's successes in learning to design for space.
The model supports traceability from stakeholders and requirements to behaviors, technical measures, and V&V activities. No EPS-specific reliability outcome is reported.
verification_validation_linkage: General system-level V&V linkage is present. The CSRM traces requirements from stakeholders to behaviors, assigns technical measures to subsystems/components for validation and verification, and includes Validation Activity and Verification Activity elements with Plan, Procedure, Conduct, Result, Status, and Active Hyperlink fields. The paper says the level of support for Mission Engineering V&V still needs evaluation. No EPS-specific verification procedure is reported.
key_findings: CSRM is a SysML-compliant MBSE reference model providing a logical CubeSat space-ground architecture without imposing physical implementation constraints.
The CSRM is not pre-populated with mission-specific stakeholders, technical measures, behaviors, or requirements; mission teams populate these artifacts for their own CubeSat mission.
The model integrates stakeholders, requirements, behaviors, architecture, technical measures, and V&V artifacts to support traceability and reuse.

The paper argues that extending CSRM to capture a descriptive model of the full CubeSat mission is feasible, but dynamic mission-performance analysis, interoperability analysis, and mission-oriented SoS implementation require further research.
Power-related factors appear in mission trade studies, including power availability, energy collection, and energy consumption, but a dedicated EPS model is not described.
The paper provides general V&V modeling support through CSRM elements, but not EPS-specific pre-development verification procedures.
limitations_gaps: The paper states that extending CSRM beyond descriptive mission modeling to dynamic analytical assessment of overall mission performance would be challenging and requires much further research.
Mission-oriented SoS implementation with MBSE is identified as requiring improvements and extensions of MBSE concepts, processes, and tools, with further research needed for CSRM application.
The level to which current CSRM V&V support addresses Mission Engineering activities would have to be evaluated.
The summary states that more work is needed to model the mission in its entirety, including metrics for evaluating alternatives and mission utility.
The paper is early-stage and solicits stakeholder input on methodologies, conceptual frameworks, and evaluation criteria.

quality.rationale: Published as an IEEE Aerospace Conference paper. It discusses challenges and further-research gaps for extending CSRM to Mission Engineering, but does not provide a formal limitations/threats-to-validity section or empirical validity assessment.

evidence_quotes.claim: CSRM is MBSE/SysML and hosted in a modeling tool
evidence_quotes.quote: The CSRM is based on Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) principles, is System Modeling Language (SysML) compliant, is hosted in a graphical modeling tool

evidence_quotes.claim: CSRM is a logical CubeSat space-ground architecture with implementation-independent components
evidence_quotes.quote: The CSRM provides a CubeSat logical space-ground architecture. The logical components are abstractions of the physical components that perform the system functionality without imposing implementation constraints.

evidence_quotes.claim: Model scope includes stakeholders, technical measures, behaviors, requirements, and architecture
evidence_quotes.quote: The CSRM integrates five overarching elements: stakeholders, technical measures, behaviors, requirements, and architecture.

evidence_quotes.claim: Requirements and technical measures are linked to validation and verification activities
evidence_quotes.quote: The CSRM provides for defining and tracing requirements from stakeholders, to behaviors, with technical measures assigned to subsystems and components to be certified through validation and verification activities.

evidence_quotes.claim: Mission teams populate the reference model for their mission
evidence_quotes.quote: The CSRM is a repository for systems engineering artifacts. However, it is not pre-populated with specific stakeholders, technical measures, behaviors, and requirements. That is the job of the CubeSat mission development team
intended to foster completeness and economies of scale associated with reusability

evidence_quotes.claim: Sharing and reuse outcome claimed for mission-specific CSRM use
evidence_quotes.quote: Development of a mission-specific CubeSat utilizing the CSRM establishes a mechanism to share and reuse components with other design activities.

evidence_quotes.claim: CSRM can feasibly be extended for descriptive mission modeling
evidence_quotes.quote: it is feasible to extend the CSRM to capture a descriptive model of the mission

evidence_quotes.claim: Dynamic mission performance analysis is a limitation/research gap
evidence_quotes.quote: extending it beyond that point to incorporate a dynamic, analytical capability to assess overall mission performance would be challenging and an area that would require much further research

evidence_quotes.claim: Power and energy are considered as trade-study factors, not as a detailed EPS model
evidence_quotes.quote: Drivers for the transformation include how much data is to be collected, storage capacity aboard the satellite, how rapidly data can be transmitted to the receiver, and how much power is available to support these operations.

evidence_quotes.claim: Trade studies include energy collection and consumption
evidence_quotes.quote: The trade studies are based on the modeling of collecting mission observations, storage, downlink, energy collection, and energy consumption.

evidence_quotes.claim: Current V&V support exists, but Mission Engineering support requires evaluation
evidence_quotes.quote: the current CSRM provides support for verification and validation activities. The level to which that supports Mission Engineering activities would have to be evaluated.

evidence_quotes.claim: Need for further work on full mission modeling and evaluation metrics
evidence_quotes.quote: more work needs to be done in properly modelling the mission in its entirety (e.g., creation of metrics that allow for the evaluation of alternatives, mission utility, etc.)

EPS-specific modeling and EPS-specific verification are not reported; power/energy appears only as mission trade-study factors. Specific graphical modeling tool is not named.
